answer: Airey puts form before colour: colour is secondary, and a logo's shape must work before any colour is added. His working practice is to design first in black and white (monochrome) and add colour only at the end. He says this keeps the focus on the concept and the shape, and it makes sure the mark still works in one colour, for example in single-colour print, faxes, stamps, embossing and newspaper reproduction, where colour cannot carry it.

The reproduced Fevicol execution has no demonstration and no headline. It relies on a single absurd, humorous visual metaphor of an unbreakable bond (the overloaded vehicle or egg style of joke), with the brand mark as the only text. It dramatises 'the strong bond' as a situation rather than proving it. The device needs a culturally literate audience that already knows Fevicol's long-running bond promise and its comic idiom, and that will close the gap and make the inference for itself. [unsure]

Godin's method says two things must be settled first: 'Who's it for?' (the specific, smallest viable audience) and 'What's it for?' (the change you are trying to make in those people). The deliverable and the deadline are neither. He says the second question gets answered badly in two ways. One is to answer with the tactic or deliverable itself ('it's for the launch', 'it's an ad'). The other is to answer with a selfish goal for the marketer ('to make money', 'to get attention') instead of a change in the audience. [unsure]

Berger separates immediate word of mouth from ongoing word of mouth. Interesting or surprising content creates a burst of immediate talk that fades. Triggers, meaning frequent environmental cues such as Cheerios or Friday, sustain ongoing talk. A one-week read can mistake a novelty spike for lasting success. A four-month read can miss a trigger-driven effect that builds slowly, or kill something whose value lies elsewhere. The right window depends on which kind of word of mouth the goal needs, immediate buzz or sustained ongoing discussion, and on how often triggers occur.

Jain describes how the post-1991 liberalisation, together with satellite television and digital technology, changed the calendar and bazaar print industry. Hand-painted oleographic calendar art gave way to computer compositing and photographic and Photoshop imagery. New producers, markets and glossier globalised aesthetics came in, and the old artist-studio and printer networks changed. This is the object most likely to be out of date because it describes a then-current, fast-moving industrial and technological situation from fieldwork done up to the mid-2000s. It is a snapshot of a trend, not a stable historical claim. [unsure]

Reverse planning starts from the future milestone and works backwards. The steps, in order: (1) identify the upcoming milestone or decision point (the usability study); (2) determine what must be true or ready for it (a testable claims-filing flow, the task scenarios, the key screens and the error and confirmation states); (3) work backwards to schedule critiques now of the things that must be settled first. So critique the core flow structure and task path, and whether they meet the filing objectives, now, before polishing any visual detail. [unsure]

In the body text Berger rejects the Gladwell-style influentials or 'law of the few' thesis. He says it is the message, not the messenger, that makes things catch on, so marketers should not chase special influencers. In the endnote he concedes something weaker: influentials may matter somewhat, but the evidence is mixed and they are hard to identify and target cost-effectively. The difference matters because the body overclaims. The book cannot be cited as proof that influencers don't matter, only as proof that content features are a more practical lever.

Samara consistently credits an underlying, intentional structure: hidden alignments, proportional relationships, a clear hierarchy and a controlled rhythm of contrast. He calls these the designer's deliberate control, which keeps a seemingly chaotic, deconstructed layout legible and coherent, while the other layout is simply disordered. The honest limit is that these are the author's post-hoc interpretive commentaries on selected exemplars. The 'hidden order' is asserted rather than demonstrated or tested with readers, so the reading risks circularity: praised work is credited with order because it is praised. [unsure]

Jain reports practitioners' rule that gods must not be shown with defined, straining muscles. Divine bodies should be smooth, soft, rounded and youthful. Their reason is that muscles signify human effort and labour, while deities act effortlessly: their power is not physical exertion, and their bodies are full of breath or grace. The trouble comes with depicting action such as battles, Hanuman lifting the mountain, or Krishna's feats. The frontal, static, iconic body cannot convey exertion, so the poses become stiff, awkward and implausible, and the naturalist logic of movement breaks down. [unsure]

A 'GoogleDoc/' folder name records the archive's storage or conversion pipeline (where the file was kept or routed), not the provenance of the text. It says nothing about whether the book content was re-typed. What settled it was inspecting the file itself: the publisher's front matter, the copyright and ISBN page, the original pagination, layout and typography, and embedded metadata that match the published edition. Direct evidence in the file outranks inference from a directory name. [unsure]

The four questions, in order: (1) What is the objective of the design? (2) What elements of the design are related to the objective? (3) Are those elements effective in achieving the objective? (4) Why or why not? The permitted variation is to work element-first: start from an element someone notices and trace it back to the objective it serves before judging it. The second question deliberately does not care whether the elements are good or bad. It only identifies which elements bear on the objective, and evaluation comes in question three.

Hopkins says that at the end of a convincing ad the reader is persuaded but puts off acting. The impression fades, the resolve is forgotten, and the sale is lost to procrastination and inertia. His device is to get immediate action: a coupon to cut out for a free sample or offer, often with a time limit, so the reader does something at once. His evidence is keyed, traced returns, where coupon-bearing ads measurably out-pull ads without them.

Berger tested whether more interesting products get talked about more. Across a large word-of-mouth dataset of hundreds of products, the result was a null: interesting products did not get more word of mouth overall. He then split the talk into immediate and ongoing. Interesting products got more immediate word of mouth but no more ongoing talk. The null was resolved by triggers. Products cued often by the environment (such as Cheerios or Friday) stay top of mind and accessible, and that explains ongoing word of mouth better than interestingness.

Carroll says perfect symmetry is static and can feel lifeless, because nothing creates tension or leads the eye. His correction is to break the symmetry deliberately by introducing a disruptive element: a small off-balance detail, a figure or an object that interrupts the mirror and becomes the point of interest. What he does not tell you is how much to break it, where to put the disruption, or how to judge when it works. That is left to intuition, with no rule and no attention to the client's purpose. [unsure]

Dwyer and Patel contrast crowded, painterly Indian posters with sparse contemporary Western posters. Indian posters carry many star faces, collaged scenes, bright colour and emotional montage. Western posters rely on a single image, minimalism and text or taglines. The reason they give for the Indian side is the film form and the star system. Hindi films are multi-genre masala entertainments whose many attractions (stars, romance, action, songs) all have to be advertised at once, and the stars are the primary draw for a large and partly non-literate, multilingual audience, so image dominates text.

No. Google's reported roughly 30% short-term sales lift is attached to ads that follow the ABCD framework as a whole: Attract, Brand, Connect and Direct, combining multiple practices, and based on Google/Kantar-type analysis. The source does not isolate the effect of a spoken brand mention, does not decompose the lift by feature, and presents it as an association, not as a controlled causal effect of any single practice. Attributing 'most' of the 30% to audio branding alone goes beyond the evidence.

Carroll's diagnosis is camera shake: the shutter speed was too slow for handheld shooting. The tell is that everything, including static elements, is uniformly soft. Motion blur would affect only the moving subjects. His responses, from strongest: put the camera on a tripod or firm support; get a faster shutter speed (at least about 1/focal length) by raising ISO or opening the aperture; and improve handholding technique by bracing yourself, tucking in your elbows, exhaling and squeezing the shutter gently. [unsure]

No. Sontag's argument is not a compositional prescription. She argues that aestheticising is intrinsic to photography: the camera tends to beautify whatever it records, and turns suffering and reality into images to be consumed, collected and looked at. That follows from the medium and the image-world, not from a photographer's framing choices. On her account a better composition would not escape it, so using her to demand a different composition misreads a critique of photographic seeing as a style guide.

The test says that if you need to explain what happened outside the frame or before the shutter fired, the picture has failed. The excuse proves the photograph does not show what you think it shows. The reasoning is that viewers get only the frame: the minute of waiting, the context and the story are invisible to them. A photograph must stand on its own, so whatever needs a caption to justify it is missing from the image.

Hopkins objects that the inquirer responded to durability. That is the argument that interested them, so the follow-up must continue on the same line that drew the reply. Switching to price abandons the appeal that worked and addresses someone the prospect is not. On timing, he says follow-up must be prompt, arriving with or right after the sample while interest is fresh, because delay lets the interest cool.

The Law of Fellowship says a leader should welcome and even encourage healthy competitors, because rivals build and legitimise the category and customers like choice. The authors bound it by noting that the ideal is a small number of strong brands (often a two-horse race such as Coke/Pepsi), not unlimited entry, and that the leader must stay the leader. The weakest link is causal: their illustrative case assumes category growth came from competition rather than from other factors, with anecdote and no controlled comparison. [unsure]

Airey concluded he should have set up a thorough upfront briefing: a design questionnaire and discovery conversation that asks explicitly about existing preferences, preconceptions and past attempts, with all the decision-makers involved from the start. His account suggests they stayed quiet because they wanted to see whether the designer would independently arrive at their idea, and treated the process as a test. They also didn't realise that withheld expectations would derail the work. [unsure]

Jain separates naturalist techniques (perspective, chiaroscuro, anatomical modelling, illusionistic rendering) from the European schemata that carried them: the academic compositional formulas, genres and narrative pictorial conventions of history painting and so on. Indian practice, including Ravi Varma and later calendar art, took up the techniques selectively. It embedded them in its own frontal, iconic, darshan-oriented schemata of devotional address rather than adopting the Western representational framework wholesale. [unsure]

Dwyer and Patel treat the poster's text, meaning the title in English, Hindi (Devanagari) and Urdu scripts plus credits, as a designed, multi-script element. Its lettering and script choice signal genre and address different audiences, with Roman or English increasingly dominant for pan-Indian and diaspora reach. For one key art, that argues for image-led design with the title handled as a graphic element in multiple scripts. The argument stops being about India in 2002 once it depends on diaspora, multiplex and digital-distribution conditions that the book only anticipates. [unsure]

Returning the sentence as a claim about Indian politics strips it of context. In Desai's essay it is a rhetorical, essayistic provocation about everyday social behaviour and culture (how democracy is lived, or subverted, in daily hierarchical practice). It is not an empirical political thesis. The record's fix is to keep the surrounding argument and essay framing with the retrieved text. The line should be tagged as a cultural-commentary interpretation rather than a factual claim, and should not be surfaced as a standalone quotation. [unsure]

Desai argues that hierarchy gives Indian society order and predictability. Everyone knows their place and how to behave toward others, which reduces uncertainty, manages scarcity and provides security and belonging. The cost he names is that it suppresses individuality, equality and merit: it breeds deference, rigidity and discrimination, and it hinders initiative and genuine democratic behaviour. [unsure]

Carroll says foreground interest creates depth. It gives the eye an entry point and draws the viewer into the scene, leading from near to far, so a flat landscape becomes three-dimensional. On how it gets into the picture, he says it doesn't appear by itself. You have to put it there by moving: get low, step closer, change viewpoint and actively search for a rock, flower or line in the foreground.

Sullivan's test is to ask whether you would ever say this sentence out loud to a friend, for example across a table or at a bar. If a real person would never talk that way, it is ad-speak. The test detects inauthentic, puffed-up 'copywriter language' with its empty verbs and clichés, such as 'discover' and 'tantalise your tongue'. It does not tell you whether the idea is good, only whether the voice sounds like a human being talking.

The case is KamaSutra condoms, entering a category defined by the government's Nirodh family-planning programme. The name had to satisfy three requirements at once. It had to shift condoms from contraception to pleasure and sex, be rooted in Indian culture so it would be legitimate rather than foreign or vulgar, and be premium and aspirational. The source reports this as the agency team's finding (Lintas, for JK Ansell), reached through consumer research and brainstorming during the brand's creation. [unsure]

Hopkins would reject it. Educating people to a new habit is still education, and a quarter of the space is simply paying for it in instalments. The cost is out of all proportion to the returns. The benefit also goes to every maker in the category, competitors included, not just to you. Advertising should be devoted to selling to people already inclined to buy, with every line aimed at the sale, not at missionary work for the whole trade.

Ogilvy explains that viewers absorbed in a good programme won't break off to find a pencil, note the number or go to the phone, so involvement in the show suppresses response. Weaker, less engaging programming such as late-night shows and reruns leaves viewers free to act on the commercial. He concludes that you should not buy direct-response media on audience size or programme quality. Buy on measured results, meaning cost per response or order.

Airey says brand style guides are the designer's responsibility. The designer should create them and deliver them with the identity, so the mark is applied correctly by others. The chain he attaches: consistent application leads to recognition, recognition builds trust, and trust builds loyalty and brand value. Inconsistency dilutes the identity and erodes that chain.

Not necessarily. Pandey's memoir is anecdotal, cultural and philosophical. Its objects mainly supply context, attitudes and illustrative campaign stories (Indian insight, emotion, local idiom) rather than testable production rules. Leaving them unbound is honest: forcing operational or Creative IR bindings would overclaim what the source supports. It is a gap only if a specific rule in it is actionable and has been missed. The default reading is correct scoping, not an omission. [unsure]

Jain argues that judging images only on representational truth (true or false) or on aesthetic quality (good or bad) imports a Western, disinterested and textual frame. That frame misses how bazaar images actually work. She proposes attending to what images do: their efficacy and their embodied, devotional and transactional engagement. She calls this 'corpothetics' as opposed to aesthetics, and it includes their power in ritual, commercial and political networks.

Ogilvy concludes that 'when you have written your headline, you have spent eighty cents out of your dollar', and that a headline that doesn't sell wastes 80% of the client's money. The hidden step is the assumption that value is proportional to readership, and that headline-only readers are worth as much as body-copy readers. The headline must therefore carry the selling message (brand and promise) by itself. The readership ratio alone doesn't establish that.

For the essential exception to SC 1.4.11 (non-text contrast), the W3C's Understanding document gives categories where the particular presentation is essential. These are logos and brand marks, flags, real-life representations such as photographs, screenshots and depictions of real objects, and data-driven graphics such as heat maps, where colour gradients encode the information. The principle uniting them is that changing the colours to meet the contrast requirement would change or invalidate the information or identity the graphic conveys: the presentation is itself the content.

Godin uses dog food because dogs don't buy it; their owners do. Performance for the end user (the dog's taste or nutrition) matters less than how the purchase makes the buyer feel: a good, caring owner. Feature-and-performance thinking misses that. The general claim is that people buy stories, feelings and status rather than specs. Marketing serves the wants and worldview of the person making the decision, not the objective merits of the product.

In 'The Image-World' Sontag names three forms of acquisition through photography. The first is surrogate possession of a cherished person or thing. The second is possession as a consumer of events, both those in our lives and those that aren't. The third is acquiring something as information rather than experience. She treats the third as the most inclusive, because through photographs anything and everything can be turned into information, classified, stored and possessed, reaching far beyond what one could own or experience. [unsure]

The source suggests that sachets won't translate as easily into toothpaste. Shampoo sachets worked because of low unit price, trial, and occasional use (a weekly wash) that matches a single-dose pack. Toothpaste is used daily, so a sachet is a worse per-use deal than a small tube and becomes inconvenient. The mechanism is the fit between pack size and usage frequency and occasion. The author offers this as reasoned speculation from the shampoo case, not as data, so confidence is low. [unsure]

The source documents Yash Raj's Mohabbatein (released Diwali, October 2000) as a staged publicity campaign. Early teaser images and posters came months ahead. Star-led posters followed, foregrounding Amitabh Bachchan and Shah Rukh Khan, then the young couples. Music release and promotion and hoardings built toward the release, with more publicity after. One dated campaign is a single illustrative case study. It shows how a campaign can be sequenced but cannot establish typical industry practice or trends. [unsure]

Carroll explains that the camera's meter reads the bright window, averages the scene toward mid-grey and so underexposes the subject, which turns the face into a silhouette. He tells you to expose for the face: spot-meter on the skin, use exposure compensation (plus stops) or exposure lock, or add fill light or flash. The cost to accept is that the window and background will blow out to white and lose detail.

Airey's tip makes you decide whether the identity needs a symbol at all, or whether a wordmark or logotype alone will do, and to decide it early, before designing. His reasons are practical. A symbol helps when the name is long or hard to read, when international or small-size use calls for a compact mark, or when the business has scale to build it. His reason does not include prestige or 'every real brand has one'. Many strong brands are wordmark-only, and a small consultancy may not need a symbol. [unsure]

Carroll's question is: which matters more in this shot, depth of field or motion? If it's depth of field, use aperture priority; if it's freezing or blurring movement, use shutter priority. The rule shows that he thinks the decision should come from creative intent, meaning what you want the picture to show, rather than from technical settings or light levels. The camera handles the rest.

The source suggests the problem is the absence of shared, explicit objectives and of a clear close: critiques aren't ending with a recap of what was discussed, the decisions and next steps, and nobody documents it. Critique is analysis, not decision-making. Apparent agreement in the room isn't a recorded decision, and each person leaves with their own interpretation. Better facilitation of the discussion won't fix it, because the failure lies in framing (agreed objectives) and in wrap-up and follow-through, not in participation. [unsure]

Bijapurkar predicts that Indian price-sensitive consumers will reject a stripped-down 'cheap version' with old technology. They want value for money: full or current functionality at an affordable price, not inferior products, and they resent being treated as second-class. The alternative she points to is re-engineering the business model and price points, for example through smaller units, sachet-style packaging, pay-per-use or low-cost delivery, so that the real product becomes affordable. Confidence should be moderate: the evidence is illustrative case-based argument from the 2000s. [unsure]

Both hold because film costume is a semiotic system, not a mirror. Clothes in Hindi film don't reproduce what people actually wear. They are exaggerated, fantastical and designed for spectacle and character. Their meanings still depend on real-world codes the audience already knows: the sari as virtue and tradition, western dress as modernity or the vamp, regional and religious markers. Film borrows and amplifies that social grammar of dress so viewers can read character, and it does not have to depict actual clothing.

The introduction cites a frame-by-frame content analysis of about fifty years of Indian TV advertising and reports headline findings on changing portrayals, such as shifts in gender roles, family depiction and themes over time. What's missing is a verifiable basis: no clear citation of who conducted it, no stated sample, coding scheme, period breakdown or figures. It functions as appeal to authority rather than evidence that can be checked. [unsure]

The penetration figures aren't a consistent series. They come from different sources, use differing definitions (households versus individuals, urban versus all-India, TV owners versus viewers) and are taken at irregular intervals. They are often unsourced or rounded. Joining them into a growth curve would mix incompatible measures and create a spurious trajectory. At most they show broad orders of magnitude, not a rate of growth. [unsure]

The book's correction for intuitive predictions has four steps. (1) Start from the baseline: how often new suppliers generally reach the top tier. (2) Form the intuitive prediction from the strong submission. (3) Estimate how well a first submission actually predicts year-long performance, meaning the correlation between evidence and outcome. (4) Move from the baseline toward the intuitive estimate in proportion to that correlation. The prediction should move only as far as the evidence's predictive validity allows. With a weak correlation, stay close to the base rate, since the exceptional first piece partly reflects luck and will regress.

As Sullivan reports Jim Aitchison's advice, the choice between writing like a letter or like a postcard is decided by how much you have to say, meaning the length and complexity of the message: much to say means a letter (long copy), little means a postcard (short copy). The claim that has nothing to do with reading is that long copy signals there is plenty to say about the product, conveying substance and seriousness even to people who don't read it. [unsure]

Hopkins had a complete, good-quality cosmetic line with products, packaging and formulations ready. What was missing was a distinctive, advertisable advantage: some unique claim or reason-why that made it different from existing brands, so there was nothing new to say. His own word for it (roughly 'distinction' or 'something unique to feature') shows that his screen for taking on a product was whether it offered a salesman's story. He did not screen on quality alone. [unsure]

Jain ends by affirming that bazaar images have real efficacy and power: to move bodies, sustain devotion and mediate commerce and politics. She immediately qualifies this. The power doesn't reside in the image alone or as a fixed property. It arises from the networks, practices, contexts and audiences through which images circulate, so it is relational, contingent and variable, not intrinsic. [unsure]

Godin distinguishes affiliation from dominance. Affiliation asks 'Who's in and who's out? Do people like us do this? Am I part of the group?' and seeks belonging and connection. Dominance asks 'Who's up and who's down? Where do I stand? Am I winning?' and seeks rank and control. The pair isn't a segmentation because everyone uses both. Which one a person applies depends on the context and the moment, so it is a lens for reading a decision, not a fixed way of sorting people.

This copy appears to have been processed after acquisition: OCR'd or converted, with the text cleaned of scan artefacts such as running headers, hyphenation breaks and duplicated or garbled passages. The record notes how many such defects were found and fixed. The remaining risk is that undetected errors persist: misread words, dropped or merged text, or broken essay boundaries. Quotations and attributions therefore still need checking against the printed edition. [unsure]

The placement is licensed by strong colour contrast. A small saturated red figure against a large neutral grey field has enough visual weight to hold attention and balance the frame from an extreme off-centre position, while the empty space gives context and tension. Freeman's diagram goes further than his text: it draws explicit balance and weight or eye-movement relationships, implying a precise, lever-like equilibrium that the text only asserts loosely. [unsure]

The advertiser announces in advance, to dealers and in the trade, that an ad will run carrying a coupon good for a free full-size package at any dealer. The dealer redeems the coupon and is paid full retail price for it. Dealers stock because they know customers will come in asking for the product with coupons. If they don't carry it, they lose that trade, and the customer, to a competitor. They also lose nothing on redemptions, since they are paid in full. Distribution is secured before the advertising runs.

Raising the light can move the reflection out of the lenses, but it isn't reliable. It brings harsh top light and deep eye-socket shadows, and the angles depend on how the glasses sit, so it often fails. Tilting the glasses slightly down helps in some cases. The book says the only solution that always works is to remove the glass: photograph the sitter wearing the frames with the lenses taken out, or empty frames.

Showing the second reviewer the first verdict and reasoning destroys independence. It creates an anchoring or informational cascade, so agreement is largely an echo rather than corroboration. The error gets confirmed, not caught, and noise and bias are amplified while looking like consensus. Because only flagged items are routed, the check also never tests false passes. The minimal change is to have the second reviewer judge blind and independently, without seeing the first verdict or reasoning, and to reconcile afterwards. That is the book's 'aggregate independent judgments'.

Freeman says the Chinese mountain-water (shanshui) scroll rejects the European single fixed viewpoint and linear perspective. It uses a shifting, multiple viewpoint that the eye travels through, with a vertical, layered arrangement of near, middle and far distances instead of one unified space. The method he reports for building one photographically is to shoot separate frames at different distances and viewpoints and assemble them vertically as a composite, stacking the distances in the manner of the traditional 'three distances'. [unsure]

Samara means readability in the sense of engaging readers and pulling them in: arousing interest and activity so the content is actually read and remembered. He does not mean legibility or reading speed. The claim is hedged ('might even') and is speculative. It is offered as a possibility from designers' intentions and argument, with no research evidence behind it, so it has low confidence.

WCAG gives the contrast ratio formula based on relative luminance and the thresholds of SC 1.4.3: 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, with 7:1 and 4.5:1 for AAA. The Understanding notes say text over images needs sufficient contrast against the background behind the characters. It doesn't give a normative method for varied or gradient backgrounds: which pixels to sample, whether to use the worst case or an average, or how to handle anti-aliasing. That measurement protocol is left to testers, who in practice check the worst-case area.

The book answers that an uneven profile is expected and informative, not a sign of error. The point of mediating assessments is to evaluate each dimension independently and fact-based, so as to avoid the halo effect, where one impression colours everything. Real options usually have strengths and weaknesses. A profile where everything looks good would more likely indicate halo or excessive coherence. The committee should weigh the uneven profile holistically at the end rather than smooth it away.

In the Yosemite Falls picture Freeman accepts cutting part of the scene, the top of the falls or the surrounding context and sky, to gain the full vertical sweep and scale of the falling water together with a foreground anchor. The tall, narrow subject in the frame format and the fixed viewpoint meant he couldn't include everything, so he had to choose between completeness and the stronger vertical dynamic and scale. [unsure]

Hopkins's verdict is that colour usually isn't worth its cost. It adds expense without proportionately increasing sales, and 'fine' pictures don't sell. The exception is when colour is essential to showing the product, for example foods, fabrics or products whose appeal is their appearance. The exception works because there the colour itself carries the sales argument. It demonstrates the product truthfully and attractively, so it pays for itself in traced results.

In his footnote Berger narrows 'viral'. He doesn't mean true epidemic spread, where each person infects more than one other and cascades grow exponentially from one seed, which almost never happens. He uses the word loosely to mean spreading from person to person through word of mouth and social transmission. That narrowing reduces the book's promises: the STEPPS principles increase the likelihood and amount of sharing, but they can't guarantee blockbuster viral cascades.

Berger defines remarkable things as unusual, extraordinary or novel: things worthy of notice. He insists on the emphasis 'worthy of remark', meaning literally worth mentioning or talking about. He reports that remarkable products and content get talked about more (from his and others' studies of word-of-mouth data), because sharing remarkable things gives the sharer social currency and makes them seem interesting.

In Jain's account iconographic correctness is a threshold condition, not a merit: an image must get a deity's attributes, colours, weapons and mounts right to be acceptable or efficacious. Correctness doesn't make it better, and it cannot make one image more saleable than another. Artists and publishers therefore check and correct iconography as a must-pass requirement. Buyers reject incorrect images whatever their beauty, while competing on other qualities such as style, expressiveness, glossiness and appeal. [unsure]

Without formal tests, the book suggests looking for good judgment: intelligence, and above all a cognitive style of actively open-minded thinking, meaning people who seek disconfirming information, update on evidence and are comfortable with doubt. It warns against choosing on confidence, seniority, status, experience or eloquence ('respect-experts' who merely seem authoritative). It reports that measures such as general mental ability and actively open-minded thinking (along with superforecaster research) predicted judgment accuracy better than experience or self-confidence.

Bijapurkar would warn against reading a decline in an age band as a change in the people. The 25-34 bracket is refilled by new entrants each quarter, so this is a compositional or cohort effect. It is also a life-stage effect (marriage, children, jobs and household budgets change consumption) and possibly a period or market effect such as new entrants or channels. 'Less brand-loyal' is only one of several explanations. Aggregate age-band data can't settle which effect it is. That needs panel or cohort-tracking data following the same individuals. [unsure]

When every entry claims a descriptor ('super', 'premium', 'best', 'no. 1'), it inflates to meaninglessness and stops differentiating. Desai observes two responses: escalation to ever stronger superlatives, and abandonment, meaning retreat into irony, understatement or new vocabulary. This must not be merged with censorship-driven euphemism, because the mechanism differs. Inflation is devaluation through over-claiming under competition. Euphemism is substitution caused by prohibition, where the underlying meaning stays intact. Different causes imply different fixes. [unsure]

Sontag says photography specialises in producing the 'interesting', a kind of surreal equivalence in which any subject, detached from its context, can be made interesting and exchangeable with any other. Her formula is roughly that to photograph something is to make it interesting, and anything can be made interesting through the camera, so meanings float free and can be attached to anything, as in advertising. The sentence showing how far the erasure goes is her remark that 'nobody ever discovered ugliness through photographs'. [unsure]

Bijapurkar argues this wasn't down-trading. The popular or mass segment had itself improved in quality and value, so affluent consumers rationally chose it as good enough value for money. Indian consumers, including the rich, are value-seekers and mix premium and popular products across categories. The error comes from assuming a hierarchy in which income determines segment, with the premium segment as the natural home of the rich, and then reading any deviation as deprivation instead of as a rational value choice.

The terms were identical, so what changed was the salesmanship: Hopkins's advertising and presentation (the copy, the argument, the service, and how convincingly and specifically the offer was presented). His general principle is that customers don't choose on the offer's terms alone but on salesmanship-in-print. Given equal offers, the one that is better explained, more specific and more persuasive wins the business. [unsure]

A plan (overhead) diagram shows only a slice, so dark-field lighting seems to need light at just two points either side of the glass. In reality the edge-defining light must surround the subject in every direction, above and below as well, or parts of the outline go missing. The book substitutes a large light source behind the subject: a big lit background with a smaller dark card or panel directly behind the glass. Light then arrives from a continuous ring around the silhouette.

Rather than trying to capture the experience in a single composed frame, Freeman approached it as a sequence. W3C (SC 1.4.5, images of text) prefers real text because users can adapt it to their needs, while images of text fix the presentation. What is lost includes resizing without pixelation, changing font family, size, colour and background (foreground/background contrast), adjusting line, letter and word spacing, and reflow or wrapping. Other losses: user style sheets, magnification without blur, and ready interpretation by assistive technology such as screen readers, text-to-speech and translation.

The Law of Color says a brand should use a colour that is the opposite of its major competitor's, to create a distinct identity. The leader naturally takes the category's most representative colour, so the new entrant should take a contrasting colour, as Pepsi took blue against Coke's red. The trade they say to accept is giving up the category's natural colour association in exchange for differentiation and ownership of a distinct identity.

Godin's loop is culture. People take their cues from their group, so behaviour spreads as norms: when people like us do something, others in the group adopt it, which reinforces the norm. The marketer's first job is to define and understand the 'us', the specific group whose culture you're joining or shaping, and then create tension that moves them to change together. The wrong way is to try to change everyone, the mass, at once, or to fight the culture head-on instead of working through a smaller group whose norms spread.

Ogilvy reports that comparative advertising naming the competitor doesn't generally perform better. It tends to be less credible and less persuasive, and it can confuse viewers, who may remember the competitor rather than your brand. The risk, as he sees it, is that you give the competitor free publicity and viewers may misattribute the brands. Demonstrations that knock the rival can also look unfair, invite retaliation or lawsuits, and lower consumers' view of both brands. [unsure]

In the first version the stars have a contrasting black outline, so the graphics are perceivable (SC 1.4.11 is met). Earned and unearned stars, however, differ only by fill colour (yellow versus white), so it risks failing SC 1.4.1 Use of Color unless there is another cue or sufficient contrast. The second version, pale yellow stars on white with no outline, fails SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, because the star shapes lack 3:1 contrast against the adjacent white. They aren't the same criterion: one is about colour as the sole carrier of state, the other about luminance contrast of the graphic.

Yes. Connor and Irizarry hold that the critique process stays the same whatever is being critiqued (visual designs, flows, content, strategy or principles). What changes is the objectives the thing is meant to achieve. Anything created for a purpose can be critiqued against that purpose. So design principles are critiqued against what they're for: whether they are clear, distinct and actionable, whether they help the team make and evaluate decisions consistently, and whether they reflect the product's goals and users.
